HIGH TIDE
Pitch ↗Evidence index

High Tide | Chemical ecology and validation

Evidence review for ENEC Advanced Technology Pioneers, 10 November 2026. The engineering use case begins after ENEC's existing offshore warning. ENEC's brief uses the name Catostylus mosaicus and a 30–45 cm bell as the design target. Treat those as requirements for prototype dimensions and the search for biological evidence. Establish the identity, size range, and condition of the animals actually arriving at Barakah before biological testing. ENEC challenge statement

The differentiator is a testable chemical-cue layer on a physical diversion corridor. Can a verified adult jellyfish detect a localized chemical gradient, turn, and sustain enough lateral motion to reach an exit more often than under the same flow alone? The first candidate is (E)-2-nonenal, an identified molecule from jellyfish chemical ecology. A brine shrimp (Artemia) conditioned water arm covers the attraction hypothesis. The prototype and any eventual field operation have separate acceptance gates. For Demo Day, show the molecule, compare hypothetical response levels in the simulation, and demonstrate the two-branch assay with inert surrogates and flow tracing. An analytical-grade compound and live jellyfish are not needed at the booth.

What the experiments actually show

Evidence and setting Result Decision for High Tide
Arai (1991), two-inflow, central-outflow aquarium Aurelia aurita and Aequorea victoria medusae favored the side containing screened Artemia. The Aurelia also favored Artemia-conditioned water or ammonium chloride in one inflow. This is direct precedent for a side preference under chemical exposure in medusae. It motivates an attraction test with water conditioned by brine shrimp (Artemia) and balanced inflows. Exact compound identity in the prey mixture, field robustness, and transfer to Barakah adults remain open. Primary paper abstract
Miura et al. (2026), chemical analysis of a marine hydromedusa In seawater associated with injured Spirocodon saltatrix integument, (E)-2-nonenal was 23× higher than in sham samples, 1-nonanol 2.2× higher, and (E)-2-nonen-1-ol 6.6× higher. For (E)-2-nonenal, n=10 per group and p=0.00094. These are between-treatment ratios for sampled chemicals in the study conditions. They provide named compounds to test, without establishing a useful seawater gradient or its strength at Barakah. Miura et al., Figures 3–4
Miura et al. (2026), contact feeding with Chrysaora pacifica (E)-2-nonenal shortened the time a Japanese sea nettle held treated dried krill at 5% and 50% pretreatment formulations. The 0.5% formulation did not produce a significant result. (E)-2-octen-1-ol and 1-octen-3-ol produced significant shortening at 0.5% too, n=15 per compound. The study reports husbandry at 15.2–15.3 °C, pH 7.96–8.08 and salinity 31–32‰. The krill contacted the tentacle after solvent evaporation. Percentages identify how the bait was prepared. They cannot establish an effective concentration in water. The endpoint was release of prey, so all directional claims remain hypothetical. The control was offered first and only control eaters were used. The new assay randomizes treatment order and quantifies turning under Gulf-relevant conditions. Miura et al., Methods and Figure 5
Miura et al. (2026), biofilm assay A sediment-derived Tokyo Bay Ectopseudomonas strain showed over 90% biofilm inhibition at the paper's 5% treatments for selected compounds including (E)-2-octen-1-ol and 1-octen-3-ol and the tested mixtures. At the 0.5% treatment, (E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal and mixtures inhibited about 80%. The selected molecules can affect a second biological endpoint. This is a laboratory result in a single bacterium and cannot establish effects in Gulf waters. Preserve the specific molecule, test and endpoint when citing the percentages. Miura et al., Figure 6
Gimenez, Carroll and Pitt (2026), predator-conditioned water Aurelia coerulea planula settlement decreased in water containing direct chemical cues from Austraeolis ornata nudibranchs. Certain residual or damage cues alone showed no detected effect. In the separate predator-diet experiment, settlement was 27.9±6.5% control, 20.5±6.3% with predators fed anemones, and 16.4±6.1% with predators fed jellyfish polyps. The diet comparison offered no further supported effect beyond the presence of the predator. This supports specific chemical sensing at settlement, with a different endpoint and life stage. The active chemistry was not resolved and local species transfer is untested. Retain as a separate, longer-term polyp-recruitment research track. Primary study
Safety in numbers? (2026), Aurelia two-choice tank Experimental jellyfish moved away from a conspecific under those conditions. Mesh blocked contact while passing chemical, visual, and flow cues. A social orientation response is possible. The test does not isolate chemistry or establish a pheromone. A known chemical cue, matched flow, and no visible animal are cleaner tests. Primary study
Lenhoff (1961), Hydra littoralis Reduced glutathione elicited a feeding reflex, with reported half-maximal response at 10 µM. A characterized chemosensory example in a hydrozoan polyp. It supports the general hypothesis that cnidarians can sense molecules. Its dose and response cannot transfer to free-swimming adults. Primary study
Neil and Askew (2018), C. mosaicus kinematics Five laboratory medusae with 2.3–4.6 cm bells, 74 swimming bouts, mean speed 36.22±1.22 mm/s and mean contraction frequency 2.18±0.05 Hz. Measure body motion relative to water. These small-medusa values are references for scale, not swimming limits for ENEC's 30–45 cm target. Treat model swimming input and added cue-induced bias as separate variables. Primary paper · Open manuscript
Malul et al. (2019), adult Rhopilema nomadica and Rhizostoma pulmo Adults swam faster relative to water against the current than with it in a flume with test currents up to 4.5 cm/s. A later field study on R. nomadica found coherent movement against waves using aerial tracking. Active behavior can change transport. Account for hydrodynamic cues and use physical tracers so ordinary rheotaxis or wave response does not get credited to chemistry. Neither study calibrated a chemical response at Barakah. Flume study · Field study
Pecunioso et al. (2026), Aurelia coerulea In a laboratory light/dark gradient, juvenile moon jellyfish showed a preference for the bright compartment and increased activity. A light-guidance comparator can use the same choice geometry. A response in juveniles of another species does not predict adult Barakah behavior. Check turbidity and effects on fish and other organisms before considering a later installation. Primary study

Use candidate cue for both attraction and avoidance hypotheses. A pheromone is a chemical signal between members of the same species. A kairomone is an interspecies cue that benefits its receiver, such as an animal using a predator's chemical signature to avoid danger. A chemical that changes feeding after contact is a feeding deterrent. A chemical that causes movement up or down a concentration gradient would be a directional cue. Chemical sensing, faster pulsing, a short-term turn, and safe sustained diversion are four separate claims. Public studies reviewed here do not establish a named pheromone, validated directional dose, or field-ready adult repellent for ENEC's target.

Molecular exhibit

Draw the exact E isomer from the identifiers below. The slash notation in SMILES encodes the double-bond geometry and is useful for checking the depiction. For the lead, a bond diagram may annotate the conjugated C=C–C=O group. This is a structural feature and does not establish a jellyfish receptor or how the response would work.

(E)-2-nonenal (E)-non-2-enal. C₉H₁₆O. 140.22 g/mol. CAS 18829-56-6. InChIKey BSAIUMLZVGUGKX-BQYQJAHWSA-N. SMILES CCCCCC/C=C/C=O. PubChem CID 5283335 · 2D structure Lead hypothesis for directional avoidance because there is both chemical identification and a contact behavioral endpoint. Treat it as a laboratory test article.
(E)-2-octen-1-ol (E)-oct-2-en-1-ol. C₈H₁₆O. 128.21 g/mol. CAS 18409-17-1. InChIKey AYQPVPFZWIQERS-VOTSOKGWSA-N. SMILES CCCCC/C=C/CO. PubChem CID 5318599 · NIST Second candidate. Although it shortened prey holding in the study at a lower nominal formulation, the authors did not detect it in injured or sham seawater samples. Keep both facts visible.
Reduced glutathione γ-L-glutamyl-L-cysteinylglycine. C₁₀H₁₇N₃O₆S. 307.32 g/mol. PubChem CID 124886 Optional educational comparator for feeding reflexes. It is neither the primary test candidate nor a known medusa attractant.
Prey-conditioned water Mixture. No single structure can represent the cue. Standardize donor prey species, food density, conditioning time, filtration and batch blanks. Attraction hypothesis. Start with natural odor conditioned in a partner laboratory, with matched controls. Presence of a signal in this arm could justify fractionation and blind retesting to identify a specific cue.

The lead aldehyde was first identified among cucumber-like odor compounds of S. saltatrix in 2019. Yoshida et al. reported an average 0.22 ppm (E)-2-nonenal in homogenized samples of three jellyfish. That result is a tissue-sample value rather than a dissolved plume concentration or behavioral threshold. The later 2026 study connected a defined series of molecules with a feeding assay and measured their enrichment in seawater after injury. The aldehyde has also been identified in brown algae and dinoflagellate cultures, so ambient chemical sampling may detect background sources. Draw the structure independently from PubChem, where the chemical identity and stereochemistry are available, and cite the Miura paper for biology. Do not confuse (E)-2-nonenal with 4-hydroxy-2-nonenal, nonanal or the two-double-bond compound (E,Z)-2,6-nonadienal. Their safety and biological data are not interchangeable. Yoshida et al., 2019 · Miura et al., 2026 · Boonprab et al., brown alga · Dinoflagellate GC–MS study

The structures/ directory contains both candidates' 2D depictions, their 3D PubChem conformers and a verified identity record for use offline. A computed conformer is a representation of molecular geometry. It contains no biological effect, receptor binding evidence or exposure recommendation.

Rejected as a design path. Ammonium chloride provides historical evidence of side preference in Aurelia, and ammonia speciation and toxicity vary with pH, temperature and salinity. It does not make sense to propose adding ammonia to marine intake water. Laboratory indoles such as 5-methoxy-2-methylindole have induced polyp-to-medusa development in some species. That is a life-cycle manipulation in the opposite direction to bloom suppression. Live predators, injured-animal extracts, antibiotics and general toxicants have no role in the proposed coastal response. US EPA saltwater ammonia evidence · Fuchs et al., strobilation experiments

Resolve the Barakah species before claiming selectivity

A UAE University dissertation reports morphological and molecular work on jellyfish collected between December 2019 and August 2022 and reports C. mosaicus among the observed taxa. A later integrative Catostylus taxonomy study illustrates a specimen identified as C. perezi from Ras Al Khaimah and places photographed C. mosaicus in Australia. The World Register of Marine Species lists an Arabian Gulf type locality for C. perezi. These findings are geographically and methodologically different. They warrant local vouchers and expert identification and do not establish that the study and ENEC labels refer to the same animal or that either taxon dominates Barakah. UAEU dissertation · Integrative taxonomy paper, Figure 1 · WoRMS C. perezi

Ask ENEC to share anonymized specimen photographs, seasonal size distributions, and the identification method. With a qualified partner, keep image and tissue vouchers of each focal test animal or lot, and compare morphology and mitochondrial COI/16S against curated references including Gulf Catostylus records. Retain accession and voucher IDs, collection date and water conditions. Mixed blooms should be recorded by morphotype even where not all animals can be identified. Preserve site confidentiality in outward-facing materials. Integrative taxonomy methods · Medusozoa COI study

Environmental DNA could help confirm presence or taxon composition after a target-specific assay is validated against local congeners. Keep field blanks, assay blanks, inhibition controls, tissue positive controls and paired visual or net observations. Local seawater chemistry, organism size, shedding, advection and decay can bias concentration. Even successful cubozoan field assays have found poor relationships between eDNA concentration and abundance. For intake loading, use paired direct counts, standardized wet-mass handling records and visual/sonar observations, where available. Bolte et al., cubozoan field validation · Andruszkiewicz Allan et al., shedding and decay

Temperature, salinity and other competing explanations

  • Temperature as a test factor. Use operator-provided local temperature profiles for the test window and acclimate animals. Temperature affects metabolism, viscosity, dissolved oxygen and chemical persistence, and seasonal differences can change the species and condition of a bloom. A separate experiment must isolate acute temperature preference from temperature-dependent survival, development, or flow. Local hypotheses should compare a cue against a matched temperature control and test more than one season-representative condition. If a thermal gradient is researched, map density-driven flow with inert tracers and distinguish active choice from a current produced by warming or cooling. Aurelia ephyra temperature and hydrodynamics experiment · Barakah-region model and buoy comparison, Khalifa University
  • Life stage changes the answer. In an experimental study of Portuguese Catostylus tagi, polyps generally did best at 17–20 °C and salinity 17.5–25 for the studied endpoints. The authors tested 14, 17, 20 and 23 °C and salinities 10, 17.5, 25 and 35. These values relate to a Portuguese congener's benthic stage. They cannot identify a temperature that Gulf adult medusae will avoid. Silva et al., 2026
  • Salinity can suppress movement through stress. In an Australian C. mosaicus study, prolonged exposure to 10‰ stopped pulsation in all medusae in that group by day five, while at 20‰ one of four was still alive from day seven onward. The original study had 20 years of estuarine observations and experimental exposure to sharp declines from a control around 34.5‰. A fishery/estuary survival experiment supplies neither an acute avoidance threshold nor a Gulf treatment. Use a matched salinity control and exclude stress-driven immobility from steering success. Loveridge et al., author manuscript
  • Hold constant or measure local salinity, dissolved oxygen, pH, light, turbidity, dissolved organic carbon, actual current and shear, prior feeding, life stage, body size, time since transfer, tank-wall encounters, tide analog, test date and cue age. These can affect attraction, distribution, chemistry or apparent detection. In a bench experiment, equal temperature and salinity in the two arms avoid a density flow that masquerades as chemotaxis.

Contained validation program

Gate Method Evidence required to advance
0. Establish the physical baseline In a small closed water-channel mock-up, compare no actuation, bubble/guide actuation, and rescue or safe-exit arrangements. Use neutral or buoyancy-characterized soft surrogates, a known inlet, side outlet and labeled retained region. Map flows and washout using video and tracers. Report incoming, intake-side, released, retained and recirculated counts separately. Validate that apparent preference between branch arms vanishes when only water flows. Retain baseline data even if the chemical branch fails.
1. Identify animals and build the assay Use a marine partner with appropriate animal care and containment. Reconfirm focal animals and test both a Gulf Catostylus lot and a comparable nontarget where authorized. Use an animal-scale choice chamber with symmetrically matched inlets, flow straighteners and separate outlets. Verify plume geometry and water residence first with tracers and validate cue exposure with chemistry samples and appropriate blanks. No organisms in the initial demonstration. Record real flow and measured aqueous concentration, including concentrations on both sides and time to washout. Control site-like temperature, salinity, oxygen and lighting. Identify likely sorption, volatilization or degradation before animal exposure. Use a qualified chemist to set contained exposures after hazard review. The feeding paper's formulations cannot set the dose.
2. Test attraction or avoidance Pre-register comparisons of solvent blank, no cue, water conditioned by brine shrimp (Artemia), lead candidate, and any second molecule. Reverse cue side between blocks, randomize order, use individual trials, track video blind to treatment and match animal condition. A spatial gradient establishes candidate directional response, a uniform concentration checks activity changes, and a recovery period checks reversibility. Block by individual, source lot, tank and day, and report handling attrition. Analyze signed flow-corrected lateral velocity and angle, first choice, time in each arm, arrival/exit fraction, residence, and re-entry. Score pulsation and contact responses separately. A candidate must create repeatable directional movement in the desired direction, rather than only change speed, feeding or settling. Check performance at more than one flow, temperature and exposure condition.
3. Test incremental value Run a pre-registered 2×2 matrix, cue off/on and physical guidance off/on, across at least two current directions and a relevant size distribution. Keep existing protection as the baseline and hold inlet water conditions constant. Quantify the difference in safe exit outcomes at matched flows. Report the incremental effect of cue + physical over physical only, with uncertainty and a holdout run. Reject if animals accumulate or return, if cue changes the flow independent of animal behavior, or if the effect requires sustained high exposure or risky solvents.
4. Prove containment and non-target margin In a closed or hydraulically isolated partner facility, sample the cue source, recovery branch, treated effluent and outlet separately. Establish analytical recovery and degradation; check relevant marine non-target endpoints and leachables. Estimate realistic exposure including plausible faults. Before any environmental trial, have ENEC and the relevant authority agree the test location, thresholds and decision criteria, and accept proof of treatment under worst credible conditions. If there is no demonstrated efficacy/selectivity margin or no suitable contained configuration, drop the chemical layer and continue the physical system.

Controls that answer the hardest judge question. A cue arm that passes more water will move more animals whether they can sense chemistry or not. A colored tracer will show advection, but its distribution will not prove the chemical gradient unless analytical sampling confirms it. Use a dry run with tracers, measure velocities in both arms and estimate animal swimming velocity as tracked motion minus local water velocity. In a Y-like geometry, repeat with the cue and blank swapped, and compare a uniform-cue trial to a gradient at comparable exposure. Fix the analysis window in advance, and report all tested animals, including no-choice observations. First-choice tests need independent animals, rather than counting repeated turns as more individuals. For a binary first-choice pilot with 30 independent eligible animals, 21 of 30 gives an exact two-sided binomial p≈0.043 against 50:50. At a true preference of 75%, that rule has only about 80% power. This is a planning example; revise the analysis for multiple conditions, animal clustering and nonchoices, and make it subordinate to the flow-corrected direction and safe-exit results.

High Tide project gates are provisional. Pre-register a minimum effect that matters for ENEC's operating window, such as a ≥15 percentage-point absolute gain in verified exits versus physical guidance alone under matched conditions. Treat this as a proposed engineering decision threshold rather than measured performance or an ENEC requirement. Agree permitted injury and welfare endpoints with the marine partner. Report response latency, recovery, 24–72 hour observations when feasible and relevant, accumulation, and intact transport. A repeatable modest lab bias may still be too small to matter at intake-approach currents.

Effects on other animals and how to manage them

The evidence reviewed establishes an effect on feeding in one other jellyfish species and on a selected bacterial biofilm under study conditions. It does not quantify ecological effects at Barakah for fish larvae, turtles, corals, bivalves, copepods or Gulf algae. For an initial laboratory feasibility decision, nontarget testing should cover a local non-target jellyfish or other cnidarian, a representative fish endpoint selected by marine specialists, marine microalgal growth, copepod mobility/survival and bivalve early development. Fish, sea turtles and sensitive habitats are exposure receptors to protect through site choice and containment rather than subjects for informal exposure. A matrix of exposure concentration and time, representative salinities and temperatures, direct behavior and recovery, and clean-water controls is more relevant than a generic claim of environmental safety. ENEC marine environmental program · ISO 10253:2024 algae test · ISO 17244:2025 bivalve test

  • The supplier's (E)-2-nonenal SDS identifies skin and eye irritation and reports limited toxicological investigation. A laboratory-use hazard classification or a flavoring use cannot establish ecosystem compatibility. Public SDSs for different preparations can include solvent or stabilizer data. Confirm the tested chemical, formulation, species, exposure period and endpoint before using any concentration in a risk calculation. The safe water concentration and effective adult steering concentration remain unknown. Thermo Fisher SDS, CAS 18829-56-6
  • A separate ingredient SDS lists the same CAS under aquatic chronic hazard category 2 and includes structure-based estimates of 5.461 mg/L fish LC₅₀ and 8.03 mg/L algal 96 h EC₅₀. These are reported ECOSAR estimates, with no Barakah test and no matched adult-jellyfish effective concentration. Round to about 5.5 and 8 mg/L when discussing their screening scale. Do not interpret these predictions as thresholds of safety, and do not substitute them for ecotoxicity assays in site-relevant water. The different SDS classifications make the uncertainty visible. Robertet ingredient SDS, Sections 3 and 12 · US EPA ECOSAR model documentation
  • Judge selectivity using two matched quantities. Compare the independently replicated minimum water exposure yielding a practical adult steering effect with the lowest credible non-target effect range after relevant duration, uncertainty factors and site conditions. The ratio is undefined until those data exist. Put measured and predicted concentrations at external receptors beside the agreed protective benchmarks. Include acute and repeated exposure, mixture constituents and degradation products. An apparent margin based only on a 50% lethality endpoint is insufficient to protect sublethal behavior or larval development.
  • For bench work, use closed plumbing and segregated effluent. A later captured side-stream concept would require a hydraulic capture test and validation of compound-specific removal, for example by evaluating activated carbon against measured breakthrough. Carbon performance in seawater and disposal costs are unknown. Physical isolation, a fail-closed source, measured outlet concentration and a no-discharge waste path are core design features for the trial. Collect spent media and test water through the partner's waste workflow. The pilot stage ends if treatment fails or plume escape, injury, accumulation or misdirection is detected.
  • Under Abu Dhabi marine water quality rules, EAD considers marine effects through environmental assessment and licensing. Discuss design boundaries and trial classification with ENEC and EAD before any marine installation. Read current permit terms rather than assuming a general water quality threshold authorizes a novel use. Abu Dhabi government's marine water quality regulation summary · ENEC environmental permit

Judge answers

Likely challenge Defensible answer
“Does this compound actually repel your target?” “We have a defined molecule with measured contact feeding evidence in a different jellyfish, and a separate published chemical-side preference experiment in medusae. We are testing whether those findings translate into directional response in identified Gulf adults. The physical corridor can run on its own.”
“What's in the demo plume?” “For the booth, an inert tracer shows the geometry. The molecule and behavioral response displayed on screen illustrate the hypothesis. We propose analytical chemistry and partner animal trials to measure the real response later.”
“Does cueing simply stun the jellyfish?” “Our acceptance measure is sustained swimming away from the intake, followed by a verified exit and recovery. Activity suppression, failed escape, aggregation and injury count against the candidate.”
“Can you use pheromones to attract them?” “An arm supplied with water that held brine shrimp (Artemia) can test attraction. We would only claim a pheromone if the active chemical were identified and shown to signal between animals of the same species. Attracting animals is useful only if the far outlet actually clears them without creating an aggregation.”
“Can we cool or warm a section instead?” “Temperature is valuable for seasonally stratified tests. A gradient in a chamber can separate choice from stress. The water volume makes heat manipulation expensive at scale, and adult preference and safe operation remain open questions.”
“How do you know if fish and turtles are affected?” “We don't yet have site-specific exposure effects. The proposal keeps chemicals in contained studies and requires real water concentrations, marine endpoints and demonstrated capture before requesting any field trial.”
“Why keep bubble or guide hardware if the molecule works?” “A jellyfish may orient and still drift toward the intake. The measured incremental effect tells us where a small steering bias complements water movement and where flow alone should be used.”
“What if you find a different species on site?” “The brief still informs design size. Our assay starts with vouchers and local species confirmation. Each confirmed common species gets a separate estimate, and no single response curve stands for a mixed bloom.”
“Where is the invention?” “The candidate molecule and bubble technology come from prior work. Our proposed contribution is linking an adult choice assay with a quantified physical diversion and recovery path, then measuring whether the chemistry adds enough improvement to warrant use.”
“What do you need from ENEC next?” “An anonymized description of the bloom and its species composition, representative current/temperature/salinity/depth conditions, candidate paths that actually clear the intake approach, an appropriate partner to run contained tests, and agreed measures for a useful effect and non-target protection.”
